items.stem: By the time of the Potsdam Conference in July 1945, relations between the Allies had changed. What was agreed at the Yalta Conference?
items.answer: Germany would be divided into four zones of occupation, and Berlin too. Free elections would be held in the liberated countries of eastern Europe. Poland would be in the Soviet sphere of influence, with its border moved west. The USSR would join the war against Japan after Germany's defeat. The United Nations would be set up. Nazi war criminals would be tried.

items.stem: By the time of the Potsdam Conference in July 1945, relations between the Allies had changed. Describe the disagreements at the Potsdam Conference.
items.answer: They disagreed over the new Polish-German border on the Oder-Neisse line. They argued over reparations: Stalin wanted large payments, Truman did not want Germany crippled. Truman objected to the communist-dominated government in Poland. Truman was suspicious of Stalin and less willing to compromise than Roosevelt. The atomic bomb increased mistrust.

items.answer: (a) They disagreed over the new Polish-German border on the Oder-Neisse line. They argued over reparations: Stalin wanted large payments, Truman did not want Germany crippled. They disagreed about the future of Germany and reparations.

items.stem: In February 1945 Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met at Yalta in the Crimea. ‘The change of American leader from Roosevelt to Truman was the main reason the wartime alliance broke down.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Truman was more anti-communist and took a tougher line at Potsdam. He used the atomic bomb as a source of pressure. Against: Ideological differences between capitalism and communism existed long before 1945. Stalin's actions in Poland and eastern Europe broke the spirit of Yalta. The defeat of Germany removed the common enemy. The atomic bomb itself created fear and suspicion. Judgement: Truman's attitude sped up the breakdown, but the deeper causes were ideological differences and Soviet control of eastern Europe, which would have caused tension under any leader.

items.stem: Stalin claimed that the USSR needed friendly governments on its western border. ‘Stalin's actions in eastern Europe after 1945 were mainly defensive.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: The USSR had been invaded through Poland twice in 30 years. The scale of Soviet losses made security Stalin's priority. He had been given a sphere of influence in Poland at Yalta. Against: He imposed communist dictatorships by force, breaking the Yalta promise of free elections. Cominform spread Soviet control over communist parties across Europe. He took resources and reparations from occupied countries. Judgement: Stalin's motives combined security and the spread of communism; the methods he used made the West see them as aggressive whatever his intentions.

items.stem: In June 1947 the US Secretary of State George Marshall proposed a European recovery programme. (a) Describe the Marshall Plan. [4] (b) Why did the USA introduce the Marshall Plan? [6]
items.answer: (a) It was proposed by George Marshall in June 1947. It offered economic aid to help Europe recover from the war. About $13 billion was given between 1948 and 1952. 16 countries took part initially, with Britain, France and West Germany receiving the largest shares. Stalin refused aid for the USSR and its satellites. (b) Europe's economy was devastated and people faced hunger and unemployment. Poverty could make communism attractive, as in Italy and France where communist parties were strong. A prosperous Europe would buy American goods and help the US economy. It would strengthen the policy of containment begun with the Truman Doctrine.

items.stem: In June 1947 the US Secretary of State George Marshall proposed a European recovery programme. ‘The Marshall Plan was intended mainly to stop the spread of communism.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It followed the Truman Doctrine and was part of containment. Poverty made communism attractive in countries such as France and Italy. It helped bind western Europe to the USA. Against: It was a genuine humanitarian response to hunger and devastation. It served US economic interests by creating markets for American goods. It was offered to all of Europe, including the USSR. Judgement: Humanitarian and economic motives were real, but the plan's timing and purpose show that containing communism was its main strategic aim.

items.stem: How far did the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan make the Cold War worse? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: They divided Europe into two economic and political blocs. Stalin responded with Cominform and Comecon. They led to the currency reform in Germany that triggered the Berlin Blockade. Against: Soviet actions in eastern Europe had already created tension. They were a response to communist pressure in Greece and Turkey. They brought stability and recovery to western Europe. Judgement: They hardened the division of Europe, but they were a response to tension that already existed rather than its cause.

items.stem: For almost a year West Berlin was supplied entirely by air. (a) Describe the Berlin Airlift. [4] (b) Why did the Berlin Blockade fail? [6]
items.answer: (a) American and British planes flew food, fuel and supplies into West Berlin. It began in June 1948 and continued until September 1949. At its peak a plane landed every few minutes. Over two million tonnes of supplies were delivered. Stalin lifted the blockade in May 1949 after it failed. (b) The airlift kept West Berlin supplied. Stalin would not risk war by shooting down planes. West Berliners refused to accept Soviet offers of food in the east. The West showed it would not give up Berlin, and the blockade became a propaganda defeat for Stalin.

items.answer: For: The airlift kept West Berlin free and the blockade was lifted. It was a propaganda triumph showing Western determination. NATO was formed and West Germany was created as an ally. Against: Germany was divided, which the USSR could accept as the price of security. The airlift was very expensive. It began a more dangerous era of military alliances and confrontation. items.stem: By 1948 communist governments controlled most of eastern Europe. (a) Why did the West see Soviet actions in eastern Europe as a threat? [6] (b) ‘Stalin's actions in eastern Europe after 1945 were mainly defensive.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer. [10]
items.answer: (a) Stalin broke the Yalta promise of free elections. Communist rule was imposed by force and opponents were persecuted. Soviet control seemed to show communist expansion was under way, as Churchill's Iron Curtain speech warned. Communist parties were strong in western Europe, for example in France and Italy, and in Greece there was a civil war. (b) For: The USSR had been invaded through Poland twice in 30 years. The scale of Soviet losses made security Stalin's priority. He had been given a sphere of influence in Poland at Yalta. Against: He imposed communist dictatorships by force, breaking the Yalta promise of free elections. Cominform spread Soviet control over communist parties across Europe. He took resources and reparations from occupied countries. Judgement: Stalin's motives combined security and the spread of communism; the methods he used made the West see them as aggressive whatever his intentions.

items.stem: In June 1947 the US Secretary of State George Marshall proposed a European recovery programme. Describe the Marshall Plan.
items.answer: It was proposed by George Marshall in June 1947. It offered economic aid to help Europe recover from the war. About $13 billion was given between 1948 and 1952. 16 countries took part initially, with Britain, France and West Germany receiving the largest shares. Stalin refused aid for the USSR and its satellites.

items.stem: In June 1948 Stalin cut all road, rail and canal links between the western zones of Germany and West Berlin. How far was the Berlin Blockade caused by the actions of the Western powers? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: The West merged its zones and introduced a new currency without Soviet agreement. Marshall Aid was building up West Germany against Soviet wishes. Against: Stalin chose to blockade a city of two million people. Stalin wanted to force the West out of Berlin. Disagreements over reparations and Germany had existed since Potsdam. Judgement: The West's policies in Germany provoked Stalin, but the blockade was his decision and aimed to force the West out.

items.stem: Traditional, revisionist and post-revisionist historians interpret the start of the Cold War differently. (a) Why can the USA be blamed for the Cold War? [6] (b) ‘The USSR was more to blame than the USA for the start of the Cold War.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer. [10]
items.answer: (a) The atomic bomb and atomic diplomacy alarmed Stalin. The Truman Doctrine divided the world into two camps. The Marshall Plan was seen as dollar imperialism. Western actions in Germany, such as the new currency, provoked the Berlin Blockade. (b) For: Stalin broke the Yalta promise of free elections. Communist takeovers used force and fraud. The Berlin Blockade was an aggressive act. Against: US atomic diplomacy alarmed Stalin. The Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan divided Europe. Soviet actions can be seen as defensive after enormous wartime losses. Mutual suspicion and ideology meant both sides misread each other. Judgement: Both sides were responsible, but Stalin's imposition of communist rule in eastern Europe was the action that turned rivalry into Cold War.

items.stem: In February 1945 Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met at Yalta in the Crimea. What was agreed at the Yalta Conference?
items.answer: Germany would be divided into four zones of occupation, and Berlin too. Free elections would be held in the liberated countries of eastern Europe. Nazi war criminals would be tried.

items.stem: What was the Truman Doctrine?
items.answer: It was announced by Truman to Congress in March 1947. It said the USA would support free peoples resisting armed minorities or outside pressure. It was prompted by Britain's withdrawal of support for the Greek government against communist rebels. $400 million of aid went to Greece and Turkey. It marked the start of containment and the end of US isolation from Europe.
